newsitem.title: FRANCE: Saint Laurent avoids catwalk rumpus at Paris shows.
newsitem.headline: Saint Laurent avoids catwalk rumpus at Paris shows.

text.p: - Fleeing noise and crowds, Yves Saint Laurent took a handful of journalists into his inner sanctum for an intimate, close-up look at his styles for next summer on Monday, the first day of Paris's ready-to-wear season.

With its gilt mirrors, crystal chandeliers and potted palms, Saint-Laurent's imposing private salon was a fitting venue for his legendary classics -- famous black "smoking" tuxedo trousers, vivid crepe sheaths of fuschia or ultramarine blue and harem trousers.
Plush brocade couches were strewn with felt hats and bright leather gloves, and tables arranged with boxes of jewelry, and rows of macrame or alligator-skin belts and luscious scarves.

As models walked by, observers were invited to touch the soft grain de poudre of a dove-coloured trouser suit, a velvety cashmere coat or a red suede safari jacket, which came over panther print drainpipe trousers.
It was all so close, one could see the braid that edged elegant evening sandals, the motif on brass buttons of a skinny redingote or the bee's nest texture of a slinky chocolate cocktail dress.

"Yves feels that his clothes are made, not to be seen on the runway, but in a close and intimate manner...to be touched," Saint Laurent's business partner Pierre Berge told the 15 journalists present.
In recent weeks he has repeatedly denounced the "bad designers, noise and delays" of the theatrical catwalk productions at the Carrousel du Louvre.

"People might consider them a success, but they also may find they are total chaos. Designers today think more in terms of spectacle than of making clothes," he told French television on the eve of the show.
Asked whether he missed the loud music and scores of fashion groupies at the Louvre's purpose-built theatres, Saint Laurent replied: "Not at all. Just the opposite. But we're just trying this out."
Isabelle Ballu's show outside on the steps of the central post office was a chilly affair in mid-autumn temperatures of five degree celsius.

But as long as the chattering of teeth didn't drown out the soundtrack, leaving her spectators out in the cold didn't seem to bother Ballu, one of a generation of young designers whose main concern is finding an inexpensive venue to stage their collections.

Pity the poor fashion victims wearing loincloth-length skirts without stockings -- they won't last out the week at this rate. But never mind the 5 degree Celsius temperatures, in Paris it's better to look good than to feel good.
"It's a nice place, but it just happens to be the coldest day yet this fall. They should have served tea, or anything hot," said one observer, huddled .
It was a poor girl's show, with imitation Missoni stretch tops over synthetic shorts, and plain blouses in thin textured fabrics with flappy sleeves.
Smooth belted dresses of beige or almond looked like nurses' uniforms when in white or spinsterly evening wear in black.
The inventive cutting -- her frequent use of darts, diagonal panelling on dress and jacket backs and biased seams -- was lost on the clothes which had a home-made, thrown together look.
